newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia needs privatization to seal success.
newsitem.headline: Croatia needs privatization to seal success.

text.p: Recovering from a devastating four-year war, Croatia has achieved stability within, but now needs to push ahead to secure stable long-term growth.

Economy Minister Davor Stern said the government was committed, despite considerable public opposition, to going ahead more aggressively with the privatisation of key public sectors that remained untouched by the process launched in 1991.
An austerity programme started in October 1993 helped Croatia slash war-induced inflation of more than 1,000 percent to no more than 3.5 percent annually in 1996.
It also stabilised the exchange rate of the then domestic currency and paved the way for the introduction of its currency, the kuna, at 3.7 to the German mark and six to the dollar in May 1994.

The aftermath of the war, combined with the loss of internal Yugoslav markets, reduced economic growth to a modest 0.8 percent in 1994. But the rebound in activity since has seen economic growth accelerate to 1.7 percent in 1995 and around 6 percent in 1996.
This rate of growth can be sustained only if privatisation, and with it competitiveness, accelerates, analysts say.

Croatia's private sector currently accounts for no more than between 50 percent and 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), and the government has committed itself in a letter to the World Bank to complete the privatisation process by 1999.
As part of the privatisation drive, the state privatisation agency will sell $2.3 billion worth of assets, most of its remaining portfolio, through a mass voucher scheme to be launched in April.
The mass privatisation, encompassing roughly 800 firms, is expected to bring in badly needed capital and result in better management.
The latter could be provided by investment funds expected to manage the majority of small shareholders' portfolios, analysts said.
"It will take a year or two for the benefits of having a clear ownership structure to become evident," said Zarko Miljenovic, chief economist at Zagrebacka Banka.

Although industrial productivity in industry rose a formidable 11 percent in 1996, according to Miljenovic's data, this did not necessarily reflect the benefits of restructuring but was due largely to greater usage of idle capacity after a long recession.

Privatisation is also a necessary prerequisite for attracting badly needed direct foreign investment. This doubled to about $280 million in 1996 but is still small compared with other emerging economies.

In a recent case underlining the danger of not getting serious privatisation rolling, San Francisco-based clothing maker Levi Strauss told the leading Croatian textile firm Varteks that it would not extend its license for Levi's jeans unless the firm was privatised by June.
Restructuring the banking sector and utilities, such as telecommunications, roads and railways, water, forestry and the country's biggest company, the oil and gas monopoly INA, is most problematic.
The government is often reluctant to let these sectors go for a mixture of economic and political reasons, even though analysts believe privatising them would benefit the economy.
"Long-term prospects for growth of the Croatian economy depend mostly on the privatisation of large state-owned banks and public utilities," Miljenovic said.

Although their contribution to the GDP is relatively small, the importance of utilities and banks is far larger because they influence the efficiency of the entire economy through the price of their services.
